rv.q: Lyndsey Turner’s production cleverly reframes the story (if you can call it that) in a modern-day care home.
The austerity accentuates the lyrical richness; Thomas’s word-music cuts to the way our identities are bundled up communally with others and our past selves, the living and the dead co-mingled.
It’s an inspired and poignant approach to the piece, the setting acutely topical and quietly assertive of the love and care due to the most fragile in society.

But the drama as a whole – beyond the father and son dynamic of the framing device – remains emotionally distant as one vignette after another is delivered and feels a little wrung out as Thomas’s language loses some of its richness (he died without having revised or edited the piece fully).

And I hadn’t read or heard Under Milk Wood , Dylan Thomas’ play-for-voices, for decades. Actually, not since those cheesy-listening tracks were the grownups’ hip-hop. I remember being thrilled aged eight to find out, against parental intention, that the village of Llareggub whose day the poet relates is a palindrome of “bugger all”.
It's thrilling to see a veteran cast light up the stage and Sheen's passionate narration allows Thomas' poetic prose to soar once more.
Such small details perfectly emulate the vague-yet-particular signature style of all our dreams.
It helps too that the "reopening" show, Lindsey Turner's production of Dylan Thomas's classic Under Milk Wood, is absolutely delightful.

cn.t: Michael Sheen delivers a commanding, hypnotic performance in this ingenious National Theatre revival that frames Dylan Thomas's poetic masterpiece within a care home setting, though critics are divided on whether the added framing enhances or dilutes the original work.
